chapter: Old New Orleans and the Twenties
title: Health routine, mother's cooking and the hot spots today
summary: Armstrong says he feels no different than before, recalls his mother's red beans and gumbo made cheaply in 1915, and says Chicago and New York have the most work for musicians.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah, well, do you feel that it used to swing more in the good old days, or is that just talking and swinging right now?

I don't feel no different now. I did that. I don't feel the better that I did now. I go through the same routine as taking care of my health. I do this when I want to. I have a little nap and take my way to. I mean, it's... In the old days in New Orleans when you were growing up, what kind of food did you have, or during your early band days? Food? Mama could cook a pot of red beans and rice, and, you know, cuvillons, and, you know, cruelled gumbo, and all that stuff, with little money. Because in 1915 the bold weavers were there. Oh, yeah. You know? And she could take 15 cents and make the biggest pot of your man. People know how to do that today, do they? Well, they got some of them. You see? Get out of work. You got to take 15 cents? Oh, from New Orleans, anybody's in cooking with little money. You were talking about New York and Chicago and New Orleans. What's the best place now? What's the hottest spot in the country? Well, I think there's more places going in Chicago now and in New York where musicians can work. It's all on the north side. Boots ain't left there in 20 years or so. Yeah. You see, I mean, there's so many spots in Chicago for you to work with in New York, and there's nothing. And that seems to be the hottest thing, but they're just over-dirty, the musicians, they got so carried away, and that's cool, and they got so important, you know, you know what I mean? You play a hospital or a chenny that's a great night. You know, well, we didn't do that. Man, that was crazy. That's the way we did, yeah.
